PAPER: RESEARCH ARTICLE Published Online: September 12, 2025 https://doi.org/10.31893/multiscience.2026211 The impact of logistics performance on agricultural exports in ASEAN Giang Nguyenab | Huy Le Vuac aKangwon National University, Gangwon-do, Republic of Korea. bForeign Trade University, Hanoi, Vietnam. cVietnam Maritime University, Hai Phong, Vietnam. Abstract Agricultural products are vital to the economies of ASEAN countries, accounting for a substantial share of total exports. Beyond generating essential income for local producers, trade in these products also contributes to addressing food security challenges. However, the competitiveness of ASEAN’s agricultural exports is increasingly constrained by external shocks, rising transportation costs, and intensifying global competition. Although logistics is widely recognized as a key enabler of international trade, its specific role in facilitating agricultural exports from the region remains underexplored. To address this gap, the present study examines the influence of logistics performance on agricultural trade flows from ASEAN countries. An augmented gravity model is estimated using Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood (PPML), drawing on detailed product-level bilateral trade data covering ten ASEAN economies and 196 trading partners from 2007 to 2022. The model incorporates multiple fixed effects to account for unobserved heterogeneity and multilateral resistance terms, ensuring consistent and robust estimation. The results reveal that improvements in logistics performance significantly enhance agricultural exports from ASEAN. Furthermore, effective logistics systems help reduce the adverse impact of transportation costs, enabling exporters to overcome geographical and infrastructural constraints. These findings highlight the strategic role of logistics in strengthening export competitiveness and resilience, particularly in the agricultural sector. By lowering trade-related barriers and improving market access, enhanced logistics performance supports not only trade expansion but also sustainable economic development and long-term agricultural growth across the ASEAN region. Keywords: ASEAN, logistics performance, agricultural exports, gravity model, poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood 1. Introduction The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) region plays a key role in global agricultural markets (Greenville & Kawasaki, 2018). The participation of ASEAN states in international trade in agricultural products not only provides critical income for local producers but also plays help tackle food security challenges (Mohd Huda & Kasim, 2022).Despite experiencing strong economic growth, the agricultural sector remains essential, contributing over 11% to GDP on average from 2010 to 2020 (Aksenov et al., 2021; Mizik et al., 2020). ASEAN aims to achieve deep economic integration through regional partnerships (Mizik, 2021). Its efforts, including the establishment of the ASEAN Free Trade Area (AFTA) in 1992 and the Common Effective Preferential Tariff scheme, seek to liberalize regional trade and strengthen economic ties among member states (Atici & Furuya, 2008). These initiatives are designed to enhance trade competitiveness, particularly in agricultural products (Hoang, 2020). In addition, ASEAN’s Free Trade Agreements with major partners such as China, India, Japan, and South Korea are expected to further boost agricultural exports from the region. These efforts coincide with significant growth in ASEAN’s agricultural exports, which surge have clearly risen from USD 63.8 billion in 2007 to USD 155 billion in 2022- a growth of 143% (Figure 1). Although there was a significant drop in 2012, the sector has proven resilience by continuing to grow, even during the COVID-19 pandemic and global economic challenges. Despite considerable trade liberalization and reduced tariff rates, high transportation costs resulting from inefficient logistics services and infrastructure remain major barriers to international trade (Hummels, 2007; Martí et al., 2014; Zaninović et al., 2021). Geographical distances further drive-up transportation costs (De Groot et al., 2004; Le & Nguyen, 2022), restricting trade to nearer partners. Existing literature highlights that advancements in logistics can ease trade bottlenecks and lessen the negative impacts of geographical distance (Çelebi, 2019; Halaszovich & Kinra, 2020; Vu & Eum, 2024). Research consistently demonstrates the benefits of logistics on international trade, such as Behar et al., 2013; Behar & Manners, 2008; Doan & Vu, 2024; Gani, 2017; Martí et al., 2014; Martí & Puertas, 2017 etc. Since agricultural products are perishable and require efficient logistics for long-distance transport and distribution (Mendes dos Reis et al., 2020), improving logistics performance has the potential to boost agricultural exports from ASEAN Multidiscip. According to Jaroensathapornkul (2021), the average value of food loss between 1991 and 2013 was equivalent to 1.6%, 0.94%, and 0.42% of GDP in Cambodia, Myanmar, and Indonesia, respectively. Despite this, studies on agricultural trade of ASEAN are quite limited in the existing literature (Mizik, 2021). Most existing studies focus on the trade relationships between ASEAN and an individual partner, such as India or China (Fan et al., 2023; Pandey & Choubey, 2021; Renjini et al., 2017), or target specific ASEAN member states (Arifah & Kim, 2022; Evangelista et al., 2022; Lim, 2024; Thang et al., 2022). In addition, the linkage between logistics performance and agricultural trade of ASEAN has received little attention from scholars, despite its significant importance. This study addresses this gap by empirically examining the role of logistics performance in promoting agricultural exports from ASEAN countries. Using product-level bilateral trade data spanning 2007-2022 for ten ASEAN nations and 196 trading partners, we employ an augmented gravity model estimated with PPML. The model includes fixed effects to account for inward and outward multilateral resistance, confirming the robustness of the findings. The results show that enhanced logistics performance in ASEAN countries significantly and positively influences agricultural exports. Additionally, improved logistics infrastructure helps reduce the adverse effects of high transportation costs, highlighting the importance of logistics in facilitating trade. By providing new empirical evidence grounded in a comprehensive dataset, this study contributes to the literature on trade and development. First, it provides empirical evidence of the positive effects of logistics performance on agricultural exports from ASEAN countries, utilizing augmented gravity models. Second, it broadens the analysis by including trade data between ASEAN countries and 196 trading partners from 2007 to 2022, thereby overcoming the limitations of prior studies that focus on a narrow set of trade relationships. Third, unlike previous research that typically uses aggregated data, this study employs product-level data at the 6-digit Harmonized System (HS) code level, enabling more accurate estimations of trade costs. Finally, it estimates transportation costs by multiplying oil prices with geographical distance and introduces an interaction term between transportation cost and logistics performance. This approach allows for country-specific assessments of logistics impacts while controlling for exporter-product-time and importer-product-time fixed effects to address multilateral resistances, offering an insight how logistics performance influences agricultural trade in ASEAN countries. The remainder of this study is organized as follows. Section 2 provides a theoretical overview of the gravity model and reviews relevant empirical literature. Section 3 delineates the research methodology in detail. Section 4 presents the data and analytical strategy used in this study. Section 5 presents the empirical results, and Section 6 concludes the study. https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Nguyen and Vu (2026) 3 2. Literature review 2.1. Gravity model of trade Inspired by Newton’s Law of Universal Gravitation, the gravity model is one of the most widely used tools for analyzing international trade (Nguyen, 2024). Its popularity stems from its solid empirical success and adaptability in accounting for various factors of international trade (Yotov et al., 2016). Early models, such as Tinbergen’s (1962), posit that bilateral trade flows between two countries are determined by their economic sizes and negatively affected by geographical distance. This straightforward framework offers an intuitive way to estimate bilateral trade, with geographical distance serving as a proxy for trade costs that hinder the attraction forces between trading economies. The basic model is generally expressed as follows: 𝑋 =𝐺∗(𝑌 ∗𝑌)/𝐷 (1) 𝑖𝑗 𝑖 𝑗 𝑖𝑗 where X denotes bilateral trade between countries i and j, Y and Y represent their economic sizes, D denotes the geographical ij i j ij distance between them, and G is a constant. Over the past three decades, the gravity model of trade has been extensively reviewed and refined, achieving more robust theoretical underpinnings (Capoani, 2023; Yotov et al., 2016). The gravity model's predictions are grounded in theories such as Ricardo's comparative advantage, the Heckscher-Ohlin-Samuelson model, and New Trade Theory (Kabir et al., 2017). Building upon the constant elasticity of substitution production function and Armington's assumptions, Anderson and Wincoop (2003) introduce a seminal structural gravity model that account for the endogeneity of prices. This advanced formulation recognizes that bilateral trade flows are not only influenced by direct bilateral trade costs but also by multilateral resistances – trade barriers with third countries. To address this issue, we employ a structural gravity model of trade to analyze ASEAN’s agricultural exports, incorporating multiple fixed effects to control for multilateral resistance. 2.2. ASEAN’s agricultural exports and logistics The agricultural sector in ASEAN holds a crucial role in the region’s economy, significantly contributing to GDP and employing a substantial portion of the population (Hoang, 2020). Agricultural exports are vital not only for income generation among local producer but also for ensuring food security for regional consumers (Greenville & Kawasaki, 2018; Mohd Huda & Kasim, 2022).Furthermore, effective trade facilitation policies and ongoing developments within the sector have enabled ASEAN countries to maintain competitiveness in the global agricultural market (Atici & Furuya, 2008; Greenville & Kawasaki, 2018). Using different measures of competitiveness, Hoang (2020) found that ASEAN countries exhibit strong competitiveness in several agricultural products, including rice, rubber, spices, and vegetable fats and oils. However, ASEAN’s agricultural trade encounters major challenges, including sensitivity to external shocks like changes in oil prices (Raghavan et al., 2024). Increased international competition has weakened the region’s agricultural trade strengths (Mizik et al., 2020), resulting in stagnation or declines in competitiveness across various agro-food sector, with notable exceptions of vegetables oils and forestry (Greenville & Kawasaki, 2018). To tackle these issues, ASEAN must continue implement policy reforms and explore new strategies to sustain its agricultural trade competitiveness amid global disruptions. Research on agricultural trade within ASEAN is conducted, but much of the existing literature primarily focuses on bilateral trade relationships or the trade dynamics of individual member states (Mizik, 2021). For example, Pandey and Choubey (2021) analyze the agricultural trade between India and ASEAN, concluding that factors like GDP and shared border positively influence trade, while distance and being landlocked hinder it. Additionally, studies by Fan et al. (2023) investigate the role of facilitation factors, including infrastructure quality and economic freedom, in China’s agricultural exports to ASEAN. Another research stream focuses on the agricultural trade of individual ASEAN member states. For instance, Nguyen (2024) investigate the determinants of Vietnam's agricultural exports to 61 countries and territories from 2001 to 2022, finding that partner countries' population, GDP per capita, trade openness, and seaport access positively influence their imports from Vietnam. Similarly, Le (2021) analyzes Vietnam's agricultural trade with 97 major trading partners, highlighting the interlinkages between globalization, logistics, and food supply in shaping export patterns. In addition, Lim (2024) examines the impact of non-tariff measures (NTMs) on Cambodia's agricultural exports to 41 countries in 2021, revealing mixed impacts depending on the type of NTMs. The literature also includes studies examining the agricultural trade of other ASEAN countries, such as Indonesia, Thailand, and the Philippines (Arifah & Kim, 2022; Evangelista et al., 2022; Romyen et al., 2023). https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Nguyen and Vu (2026) 4 Despite existing studies, the relationship between logistics and ASEAN’s agricultural trade remains underexplored. Logistics is vital for enhancing the efficiency of agricultural exports due to the perishable nature of many agricultural products (Mendes dos Reis et al., 2020). The impact of logistics on agricultural trade is substantial, as these products require timely delivery. Improvements in logistics can mitigate the negative effects of geographical distance and enhance a country’s competitiveness in trade (Çelebi, 2019; Halaszovich & Kinra, 2020; Martí et al., 2014; Martí & Puertas, 2017). It plays a crucial role in international trade by facilitating the efficient movement of goods from their origin to foreign markets (Gani, 2017). At a national level, robust logistics capabilities boost a country’s global competitiveness (Polat et al., 2023). While existing literature addresses the relationship between logistics and ASEAN trade (e.g., Ardine et al., 2023; Lai et al., 2019; Nguyen et al., 2016), there is a limited focus on its specific impact on agricultural trade. Therefore, further research is necessary to understand how logistics influences ASEAN’s agricultural exports. This study aims to fill this gap by providing empirical evidence on the effects of logistics on agricultural trade in ASEAN. 3. While importer- product-year fixed effects control for destinations' inward multilateral resistances, they do not fully account for exporting countries' outward multilateral resistances when only exporter-product and year fixed effects are included. Data and analysis strategy This study utilizes bilateral trade data at the 6-digit HS code level for exports from ten ASEAN countries to 196 importers, sourced from the Centre d'Études Prospectives et d'Informations Internationales (CEPII) BACI dataset. Following the classification used by Mizik et al. (2020) and Pandey and Choubey (2021) , we define agricultural trade as encompassing products within HS chapters 1 to 24. Analyzing data at this disaggregated product level improves the precision of trade factor estimates (Yotov et al., 2016). To measure the logistics development level of ASEAN countries, we employ the Logistics Performance Index (LPI) developed by the World Bank (WB). The LPI is a comprehensive benchmark of national logistics performance for over 160 countries, surveyed and published by the WB since 2007 (Arvis et al., 2018). This widely-used indicator has been utilized in numerous studies in the literature (Çelebi, 2019; Doan & Vu, 2023; Gani, 2017; Le, 2021; Martí et al., 2014; Martí & Puertas, 2017; Puertas et al., 2014; Vu & Eum, 2024). To date the WB has published the LPI for the years 2007, 2010, 2012, 2014, 2016, 2018, and 2023. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, the latest LPI edition (published in 2023) reflects data from the preceding year. Consequently, this study utilizes data from 2007 to 2022. To address data gaps in the LPI series, we employ linear interpolation to utilize all available information from the trade data. Control variables, including GDP and population, were sourced from the WB World Development Indicator database. Data on geographical distance, regional trade agreements, common borders, common languages, common colonizers, and colonial relationships were obtained from the CEPII gravity database. Tariff data were collected from the World Integrated Trade Solution (WITS) database. Table 1 presents the summary statistics for the variables in the standard specification. Product-level trade analyses frequently encounter the issue of zero trade flows (Yotov et al., 2016). This study faces a similar challenge, as evidenced in Table 1. The Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood (PPML) estimator is a widely recommended method for handling trade data with zero trade flows. Introduced by Silva and Tenreyro (2006), PPML allows for estimating the gravity model in multiplicative form without requiring logarithmic transformation. The stochastic general form of the gravity model can be expressed as: 𝑦=exp(𝑥𝛽)+𝜀 =exp⁡(𝑥𝛽)𝜂 (7) The constant-elasticity specification in Equation (7) represents the relationship between the non-negative trade value 𝑦 on the left-hand side and the vector of regressors 𝑥 on the right-hand side. The function 𝑒𝑥𝑝(𝑥𝛽) denotes the conditional expectation of 𝑦 given 𝑥, that is, 𝐸[𝑦|𝑥]. The error term 𝜀 satisfies 𝐸[𝜀|𝑥]=0. Define 𝜂 ≡1+𝜀/𝑒𝑥𝑝(𝑥𝛽) as a multiplicative error term such that 𝐸[𝜂|𝑥]=1. Assuming that 𝑦 is strictly positive, the model can be linearized by taking the natural logarithm of both sides: ln(𝑦)=𝑥𝛽+ln⁡(𝜂) (8) https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Nguyen and Vu (2026) 6 In Equation (8), the least squares estimator is consistent for 𝛽 if 𝑥 and 𝑙𝑛(𝜂) are uncorrelated. However, since 𝜂 =1+ 𝜀/𝑒𝑥𝑝(𝑥𝛽), 𝑙𝑛(𝜂) is generally correlated with 𝑥, except under highly restrictive assumptions. Consequently, least squares estimators based on Equation (8), whether using ordinary least squares, fixed effects, or random effects specifications, are typically inconsistent. To address this limitation, Silva and Tenreyro (2006) proposed an alternative approach based on the moment conditions: 𝐸[(𝑦−exp(𝑥𝛽))𝑥]=0 (9) The estimator implied by Equation (9) corresponds to the PPML estimator. Although the trade value 𝑦 does not follow a Poisson distribution, the estimator remains consistent because it relies on the correct specification of the conditional mean rather than the full distribution. Importantly, since 𝑦 is maintained in its level form, the PPML estimator accommodates zero trade flows, whereas the log-linearized model in Equation (8) would exclude such observations due to the undefined logarithm of zero. Furthermore, the PPML estimator is robust and efficient in the presence of heteroskedasticity, multicollinearity, and serial correlation (Álvarez et al., 2018; Egger & Nigai, 2015; Santos Silva & Tenreyro, 2011). Therefore, this study employs the PPML estimator for all empirical estimations. 5. Empirical results 5.1. Full controls for multilateral resistance terms We completely account for multilateral resistances in Equation (6) by integrate both exporter-product-year and importer-product-year fixed effects. This approach eliminates all variables that vary across exporter-time or importer-time. While we are unable to directly capture the effect of the key variable, exporting logistics performance, we can estimate its impact indirectly through its interaction with transportation costs. In Column (1) of Table 3, the transportation cost variable is included without the interaction term. The results indicate a negative effect of transportation costs on ASEAN’s agricultural exports. Specifically, a 1% increase in transportation costs is associated with an approximate 0.73% decrease in export values. This negative effect becomes stronger when we include the interaction term between transportation costs and the logistics performance of ASEAN countries, as demonstrated in Columns (2) and (3). Discussion This study examines the impact of logistics performance on the agricultural exports from ASEAN countries. Using panel bilateral trade data at the 6-digit HS product level from 10 ASEAN member states to 196 trading partners spanning 2007 to 2022, we find robust evidence of the positive effects of logistics performance on agricultural exports within the framework of standard gravity models. Additionally, our advanced models, which fully control for multilateral resistances, reveal that logistics performance plays a crucial moderating role in mitigating the negative effects of transportation costs. These findings remain consistent across models incorporating interpolated LPI values and alternative tariff variables. Our study contributes novel empirical evidence at the product level, exploring the linkage between logistics performance and agricultural exports for all ASEAN member states and their trading partners. This comprehensive approach distinguishes our work from prior studies, which typically focus on bilateral trade relationships between ASEAN and a specific https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Nguyen and Vu (2026) 9 partner (Fan et al., 2023; Pandey & Choubey, 2021; Renjini et al., 2017) or single ASEAN members (Arifah & Kim, 2022; Evangelista et al., 2022; Lim, 2024; Thang et al., 2022). Moreover, we fully address multilateral resistances by employing exporter-product-year and importer-product-year fixed effects, and we explicitly estimate the interaction between logistics performance and transportation costs. In contrast, previous studies have only partially accounted for multilateral resistances (Ardine et al., 2023; Mendes dos Reis et al., 2020; C. Van Nguyen, 2024). 7. Conclusions This study examined the role of logistics performance in shaping ASEAN’s agricultural exports using product-level bilateral trade data and augmented gravity models with PPML estimation. The analysis shows that logistics performance has a significant positive effect on agricultural exports from ASEAN countries. Efficient logistics systems also reduce the negative impact of transportation costs, effectively bringing ASEAN exporters closer to their markets. In addition to these findings, the study advances the literature by providing comprehensive evidence covering all ASEAN members and a wide set of trading partners between 2007 and 2022. By combining product-level data with a rigorous specification that accounts for multilateral resistances, the analysis delivers robust confirmation of logistics as a strategic determinant of agricultural trade in the region. The study’s findings suggest that, despite recent progress, policymakers should continue to prioritize logistics development through infrastructure investment, streamlined customs procedures, and enhanced service capacity. Regional cooperation aimed at aligning logistics-related regulations and improving cross-border connectivity can further increase efficiency and resilience, thereby supporting trade growth and food security. Although this study focuses on overall logistics performance, future research could examine specific components such as infrastructure quality, customs efficiency, digitalization, and cold chain capacity. Disaggregating by product categories or country groups would also help uncover heterogeneous effects of logistics on trade, providing more targeted guidance. Such extensions would enrich understanding of how logistics improvements can best support agricultural export growth and sustainable development in the region. Ethical considerations Not applicable. JSON: Name: asean_logistics_agri_exports_ppml Title: Estimating the effect of national logistics performance on ASEAN agricultural exports using an augmented structural gravity model with Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood Short Hypothesis: Higher logistics performance in an ASEAN exporting country causes higher bilateral agricultural export values and reduces the negative elasticity of exports with respect to transportation costs. Related Work: Empirical trade studies typically use structural gravity frameworks to estimate determinants of bilateral flows and address zero trade observations with PPML. Prior work has measured logistics with aggregate indicators and shown positive associations between logistics performance and aggregate exports, but often at country or regional aggregation. Several studies control for multilateral resistance partially (exporter-time or importer-time fixed effects) or use fewer fixed effects, which can bias estimates; others rely on bilateral or single-country analyses that limit external validity. Common limitations include use of aggregated trade data (masking product heterogeneity), incomplete treatment of multilateral resistance, limited treatment of transportation cost proxies, and sparse handling of zero flows or heteroskedasticity. Few studies estimate interactions between logistics measures and transportation-cost proxies at disaggregated product (HS6) level across a comprehensive set of partners and years, leaving unresolved how logistics mitigates distance-driven cost effects on perishable agricultural products. Abstract: This research quantifies how exporter-side logistics performance affects bilateral agricultural exports from ASEAN countries by estimating an augmented structural gravity model with Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood (PPML). Using product-level (HS6) bilateral exports from ten ASEAN exporters to global partners for 2007–2022, the model incorporates high-dimensional fixed effects to control inward and outward multilateral resistance and addresses zero trade flows and heteroskedasticity via PPML. We introduce a transportation-cost proxy (distance times oil price) and estimate its interaction with national logistics performance to identify mitigation effects. The main contribution is a rigorous, product-disaggregated assessment that isolates the elasticity of agricultural exports to logistics and quantifies how logistics attenuates the negative impact of transportation costs. Expected outcomes include precise elasticity estimates, evidence that improved logistics raises export values and reduces transport-cost sensitivity, and policy-relevant implications for infrastructure and facilitation investments to strengthen agricultural export competitiveness in ASEAN. Experiments: Datasets: (1) CEPII BACI bilateral exports at HS6 for chapters 1-24 (agricultural products), exporters=10 ASEAN members, importers=196, years=2007-2022; (2) World Bank Logistics Performance Index (LPI) cross-year values (2007,2010,2012,2014,2016,2018,2023) with linear interpolation to create annual exporter-year LPI; (3) World Development Indicators for exporter GDP and population; (4) CEPII gravity variables (geodesic distance, common border, common language, colonial ties, RTA indicators); (5) WITS product-level tariffs (minimum and weighted effective rates); (6) IMF Brent oil price series for TCOST construction. Baselines: (A) Log-linear OLS gravity excluding zero flows; (B) PPML with standard exporter-product and importer-product-year fixed effects (no TCOST interaction); (C) PPML with TCOST but without interaction; (D) Proposed PPML with TCOST and TCOST*LPI interaction and exporter-product-year + importer-product-year fixed effects. Evaluation metrics: coefficient point estimates and robust clustered standard errors for variables of interest (LPI, TCOST, interaction), p-values, pseudo R-squared, Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), out-of-sample predictive accuracy (root mean squared prediction error and mean absolute percentage error) via hold-out year cross-validation, and marginal effects of LPI on export elasticity and on TCOST elasticity. Experimental setup: estimate all regressions via PPML with high-dimensional fixed effects solver; cluster standard errors by exporter-importer-product; run three sample variants: pre-pandemic panel (2007-2018 LPI years), full panel with interpolated LPI (2007-2022), and pandemic-inclusive panel. Ablation and robustness studies: (1) replace LPI with its subcomponents (infrastructure, customs, tracking, timeliness) to test heterogeneity; (2) replace TCOST construction with distance-only and oil-only specifications; (3) alternative tariff measures: minimum vs weighted effective tariffs; (4) remove TCOST*LPI interaction to compare marginal effect estimates; (5) run sectoral placebo regressions on non-agricultural HS chapters to test specificity; (6) instrumented specification using lagged logistics or regional logistics averages as instruments for LPI to probe endogeneity (if valid instruments available). Report coefficient elasticity estimates, marginal effects plots, and prediction metrics for each model and ablation. Risk Factors and Limitations: Measurement error and temporal sparsity in LPI (interpolation bias); LPI is an aggregate national index that may mask subnational and modal heterogeneity relevant to perishable agricultural goods; potential endogeneity and reverse causality between exports and logistics improvements leading to biased coefficients if instruments are weak or invalid; omitted variable bias from unobserved trade facilitation policies or product-level quality attributes; TCOST proxy (distance × oil price) is a reduced-form approximation that may misrepresent actual transport costs and modal shares; zero-inflation and overdispersion patterns may violate PPML assumptions in subsets of the data; computational challenges and convergence issues with very high-dimensional exporter-product-year and importer-product-year fixed effects at HS6 resolution; limited generalizability outside ASEAN or to services and non-agricultural goods; tariff data inconsistencies and missing rates at HS6 leading to measurement noise; heterogeneous perishability and cold-chain requirements across agricultural products that the aggregated model may not capture; results are correlational absent a credible exogenous shock or instrument to identify causal effects fully.
